newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy car market shows glimmer of improvement - CSP.
newsitem.headline: Italy car market shows glimmer of improvement - CSP.

text.p: Italy's car market is showing slight signs of recovery despite a sharp fall of new registrations in November, auto sector research group CSP said.
Transport Ministry figures on Tuesday showed Italian new car registrations fell 11.44 percent to 134,000 in November against 151,313 registrations in November 1995.

But CSP noted that last month's data were anomalous in that in November 1995 registrations rose sharply due to a resumption of deliveries after an October strike by car-carrying truck drivers which paralysed deliveries that month leading to new car registrations of just 117,600 units.
CSP said it was necessary to look at combined sales in the two months of October and November this year to correctly evaluate the market trend.
In this way, while October and November 1995 registrations totalled 268,973 new registrations in October and November this year showed a combined total of 278,500, a 3.5 percent rise.
"So we're looking at a picture of substantial stagnation but with a very slight positive trend," CSP said in a statement, referring to its latest monthly poll of dealers' views.
Looking at orders, the percentage of dealers seeing low levels of new car buying fell in November to 38 percent, against 52 percent in October and 75 percent in July.
On short-term demand expectations, the picture here also showed a slight improvement, CSP said, with the majority of dealers polled in November seeing demand unchanged at current low levels.
But compared with October, the percentage of dealers expecting the situation to deteriorate over the next three or four months fell to 22 percent from 42 percent.

But CSP director Giamprimo Quagliano said the current phase of stagnation had not yet been fully overcome. "There is clearly a need for measures to boost the car market, even if they are only of a temporary nature," he added.
CSP has been one of the leading voices calling for some form of government incentives to revive the depressed domestic car market.
But Prime Minister Romano Prodi appeared to dash the hopes of the auto sector at the weekend when he said he did not believe special financial incentives were the best way to boost car sales.
